blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 2 (Atomic Structure), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe Moseley's observation that established the atomic number. Define nucleon number and show how the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons are found for an atom and for its ions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Moseley's observation (1913): when different elements were bombarded with cathode rays, X-rays of some characteristic frequencies were produced. The square root of the frequency of these X-rays was directly proportional to the atomic number Z:
√ν ∝ Z
He concluded that the atomic number Z is a fundamental property of an element. It is also called proton number.

Nucleon number: the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus together is the nucleon number (A), also called mass number.
A = Z + N, so N = A − Z
An atom of element X is written with A at the top left and Z at the bottom left of the symbol, e.g. ²⁷₁₃Al: Z = 13, A = 27, N = 27 − 13 = 14.

Ions: only electrons are lost or gained; protons and neutrons stay the same.
• ²⁷₁₃Al loses three electrons → Al³⁺: protons 13, neutrons 14, electrons 13 − 3 = 10.
• ³⁵₁₇Cl gains one electron → Cl⁻: protons 17, neutrons 18, electrons 17 + 1 = 18.
• Table 2.1: O²⁻ (8 n, 8 p, 10 e), S²⁻ (16 n, 16 p, 18 e), P³⁻ (16 n, 15 p, 18 e).
Thus atomic number and proton number represent the same concept.

book_ref.quote: He concluded that this number, i.e. the atomic number Z was a fundamental property of an element.

blocks.prompt: 2 Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in each of the following: (i) ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺ (ii) ¹⁹₉F⁻ (iii) ⁵⁶₂₆Fe²⁺ (iv) ⁷⁹₃₅Br⁻. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Protons = Z; neutrons = A − Z; electrons = Z minus the positive charge, or Z plus the negative charge.

book_ref.quote: Number of neutrons in an atom can be calculated as

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the behaviour of electrons, protons and neutrons in an electric field. How is the amount of deflection measured? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The behaviour of particles in an electric field depends upon their mass and charge. When beams of electrons, protons and neutrons pass one by one at the same speed through an electric field (Figure 2.1):
• Neutrons, being neutral, are not deflected but travel in a straight path perpendicular to the direction of the field.
• Protons, being positively charged, are deflected towards the negative plate.
• Electrons, being negatively charged, are deflected towards the positive plate, to a greater extent, since they are 1/1836 times as heavy as protons.

Measurement of deflection: the deviation from the original direction is measured in two ways:
(i) Angle of deflection ∝ charge/mass
(ii) Radius of deflection ∝ mass/charge
The radius is used by imagining that after deflection the particle moves in a circular path. Hence the factors affecting the radius of deflection are reciprocal to those for the angle of deflection: the light electron has a large angle and a small radius; the heavy proton a small angle and a large radius.

book_ref.quote: The behaviour of particles in an electric field depends upon their mass and charge.

blocks.prompt: 4 Give the charges (in coulomb and relative) and masses (in kg and amu) of the three fundamental particles. Which particle is the heaviest and which the lightest? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Table 2.2 gives the properties of the electron, proton and neutron. The neutron is the heaviest (1.0087 amu), just heavier than the proton (1.0073 amu); the electron is the lightest (5.4858 × 10⁻⁴ amu), about 1/1836 of the proton's mass. Proton and electron carry equal and opposite charges; the neutron has none.

book_ref.quote: The Table (2.2) shows the properties of three fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 5 Using the charges and masses in Table 2.2, calculate the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron and of the proton. How many times larger is the angle-of-deflection factor of the electron than that of the proton? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Angle of deflection ∝ charge/mass, so compare the two e/m values.

book_ref.quote: Table 2.2 Properties of three fundamental particles

steps: Ratio = (1.759 × 10¹¹)/(9.579 × 10⁷) = 1836 (equal to m_p/m_e, since the charges are equal in size).
So the electron's charge/mass, and hence its angle-of-deflection factor, is 1836 times that of the proton; its radius of deflection is correspondingly smaller.
blocks.final_answer: e/m (electron) = 1.759 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹; e/m (proton) = 9.579 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹; ratio = 1836.

blocks.prompt: 6 What are atomic emission and atomic absorption spectra? Explain why atomic spectra are called the finger prints of the elements. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Atomic emission spectrum: when an element in its gaseous state is heated to high temperatures or subjected to electrical discharge, radiation of certain wavelengths is emitted. The spectrum of this radiation contains coloured lines and is called the atomic emission spectrum (e.g. hydrogen, Figure 2.2 (a)).

Atomic absorption spectrum: when a beam of white light is passed through a gaseous sample of an element in the cold state, certain wavelengths are absorbed. The absorbed wavelengths show up as dark lines on the spectrum (Figure 2.2 (b)). The wavelengths of the dark lines are exactly the same as those of the coloured lines in the emission spectrum. (The visible hydrogen lines are at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm.)

Finger prints: each element has a unique arrangement of electrons and thus a unique range of fixed energy levels. So the wavelengths and frequencies of radiation absorbed or emitted when electrons jump from one energy level to another must also be unique. Every element therefore has its own characteristic spectrum and is identified by it (Figure 2.3); hence atomic spectra are the finger prints of the elements.

book_ref.quote: Each element has a unique arrangement of electrons and thus a unique range of fixed energy levels.

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain how the first ionization energies of elements vary down a group and across a period, giving the reasons. Which elements have the lowest and highest values in each period? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A plot of first ionization energies against atomic number (Figure 2.5, first 88 elements) shows:

1. All ionization energies are strongly endothermic: it takes energy to separate an electron from an atom.

2. Down a group (e.g. He → Ne → Ar, or Li → Na → K) ionization energies decrease. The larger the atom, the easier it is to separate an electron. Down the group the number of shells increases, the hold of the nucleus on the valence electrons decreases, and removal of electrons becomes easier.

3. Across a period ionization energies generally increase. The shell number remains the same; as the proton number increases, electrons are added to the same shell, so the nucleus attracts the valence electrons more strongly.

4. In each period the group 1 elements (alkali metals) have the lowest ionization energy and the noble gases the highest.

book_ref.quote: The second way in which ionization energies show us the details of electronic configuration

blocks.prompt: 8 The first four successive ionization energies of an element Y are 496, 4562, 6910 and 9543 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the ratio of each ionization energy to the one before it, and deduce the number of electrons in the outermost shell of Y and its group. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: A very large jump means the next electron comes from an inner shell, closer to the nucleus; count the electrons removed before the jump.

book_ref.quote: The successive ionization energies show clearly the arrangement of electrons in shells around the nucleus.

steps: The only large jump is between the first and second ionization energies, so only one electron is in the outermost shell; the second comes from an inner shell. One valence electron: group 1 (alkali metal).
blocks.final_answer: Ratios 9.20, 1.51, 1.38; Y has 1 valence electron and is in group 1.

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the azimuthal quantum number. Give its values for n = 1 to 4, the subshells they represent and the number of electrons each subshell can hold. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number ℓ can have integral values 0 to (n − 1) for each value of n. It describes the shape of the orbital.
• n = 1: ℓ = 0 only
• n = 2: ℓ = 0 and 1
• n = 3: ℓ = 0, 1 and 2
• n = 4: ℓ = 0, 1, 2 and 3
The values ℓ = 0, 1, 2, 3 are designated s, p, d, f (sharp, principal, diffused, fundamental), spectral terms used to describe features of spectral lines.

Subshell: the set of orbitals that have the same n and ℓ values. The number of subshells in a shell equals its shell number (K: 1s; L: 2s, 2p; M: 3s, 3p, 3d; N: 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f).
Electrons in a subshell = 2(2ℓ + 1):

book_ref.quote: The values of ‘ℓ’ are integers that depend on the value of the principal quantum number.

blocks.prompt: 10 For the N shell (n = 4), calculate (i) the number of subshells, (ii) the number of orbitals in each subshell and in the shell, and (iii) the maximum number of electrons in each subshell and in the shell. Show that the total agrees with 2n². (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Subshells = n; orbitals in a subshell = 2ℓ + 1; electrons in a subshell = 2(2ℓ + 1); shell total = 2n².

book_ref.quote: The number of subshells in a shell is equal to its shell number.

steps: Check: 2n² = 2 × 4² = 32, the same as the total.

blocks.prompt: 11 Explain the magnetic quantum number. Give its values for the s, p, d and f subshells and explain the term degenerate orbitals. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The magnetic quantum number m describes the orientation of an orbital in space. Within a subshell, m depends on ℓ: for a value of ℓ there are (2ℓ + 1) integral values of m, from −ℓ through 0 to +ℓ. The values of m give the number of orbitals in a subshell.

Degenerate orbitals: orbitals of the same subshell have the same energy and are called degenerate orbitals. They are differentiated from each other in the presence of a magnetic field, hence the name magnetic quantum number. The splitting of fine spectral lines in a magnetic field indicates the presence of orbitals in subshells.

book_ref.quote: Within a subshell, the value of m depends on the value of ℓ.

blocks.prompt: 12 Explain the spin quantum number. State Pauli's exclusion principle and apply it to the two electrons of a helium atom. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Spin quantum number: electrons are thought of as spinning around their own axes, as the Earth does. According to electromagnetic theory a spinning charge generates a magnetic field, so the electron behaves like a magnet. There are two possible spins, clockwise and anticlockwise (Figure 2.8). To take spin into account a fourth quantum number, the spin quantum number s, is introduced. Its values are +½ (clockwise, arrow ↑) and −½ (anticlockwise, arrow ↓).
Each orbital can accommodate at the most two electrons, provided they have opposite spins. Three quantum numbers describe an orbital; the fourth differentiates the two electrons in it.

Pauli's exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all four quantum numbers; or, two electrons in an orbital always have opposite spins.

Helium: its two electrons are in the 1s orbital:
Electron 1: n = 1, ℓ = 0, m = 0, s = +½ (clockwise)
Electron 2: n = 1, ℓ = 0, m = 0, s = −½ (anticlockwise)
They have the same n, ℓ and m but different s, i.e. their spins are opposite.

book_ref.quote: To take the electron spin into account, it is necessary to introduce a fourth quantum number

blocks.prompt: 13 Define an atomic orbital. Describe the shapes of the s and p orbitals. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Atomic orbital: the three-dimensional region in space around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum.

s orbital (ℓ = 0): the shape is spherical. The electron density around the nucleus is uniformly distributed in all directions. As the principal quantum number increases, the s orbital becomes larger; the boundary surface of 2s is larger than that of 1s. An s subshell has only one orbital (m = 0).

p orbitals (ℓ = 1): the electron density of a 2p orbital is not distributed in a spherically symmetric fashion as in an s orbital. A p orbital has two lobes on an axis (dumbbell shape). There are three p orbitals (m = −1, 0, +1), named px, py and pz according to the axes along which they lie (Figure 2.6). The three p orbitals of a subshell are degenerate.

book_ref.quote: An atomic orbital is defined as the three dimensional region in space around the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the shapes and orientations of the five d orbitals. What does the chapter say about the f orbitals? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
d orbitals (ℓ = 2): m = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, so there are five d orbitals. In a given shell they have different shapes and orientations in space (Figure 2.7, five 3d orbitals); the general shape is cloverleaf (double dumbbell).
• dxy lies in the xy plane.
• dxz lies in the xz plane.
• dyz lies in the yz plane.
• dx²−y²: its lobes lie along the x and y axes.
• dz²: two lobes along the z-axis and a 'doughnut' in the xy plane.
The five d orbitals of a subshell are degenerate and hold 10 electrons.

f orbitals (ℓ = 3): an f subshell has seven orientations in space (m = −3 to +3), i.e. there are seven f orbitals, holding 14 electrons. Their shapes are very complicated.

book_ref.quote: The shapes for the five d orbitals

blocks.prompt: 15 What is electronic configuration? Explain how it is written in shells, in subshell notation and as an orbital diagram, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons among the available shells, subshells or orbitals of an atom or ion.

In shells: the shells K, L, M, N … correspond to n = 1, 2, 3, 4 …, with capacities K 2 (1s), L 8 (2s, 2p), M 18 (3s, 3p, 3d) and N 32 (4s, 4p, 4d, 4f). E.g. H: 1s¹ (K shell); He: 1s² (K shell); Na: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ (K, L and M shells).

Subshell notation: the subshell symbols are listed one after the other, each with a superscript on the right giving the number of electrons in that subshell. E.g. ⁹₄Be, with two electrons in 1s and two in 2s, is written 1s²2s².

Orbital diagram: each group of orbitals is labelled by its subshell notation and each electron is shown by an arrow, pointing up for s = +½ and down for s = −½. E.g. boron (¹¹₅B): 1s ↑↓, 2s ↑↓, 2p ↑ _ _.

book_ref.quote: In case of subshells, the electronic configuration is described by a notation

blocks.prompt: 16 State the Aufbau principle. Explain the (n + ℓ) rule for arranging subshells in order of energy, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Aufbau (building up) principle: the subshells in an atom are filled with electrons in increasing order of their energy values.

(n + ℓ) rule: in the absence of a magnetic field the energy of a subshell depends on n and ℓ, so the order of filling is obtained from (n + ℓ):
1. The subshell with the lower (n + ℓ) value has lower energy and is filled first. E.g. 4s: 4 + 0 = 4; 3d: 3 + 2 = 5; so 4s is filled before 3d.
2. If two subshells have equal (n + ℓ), the one with the lower n is filled first. E.g. 4p: 4 + 1 = 5 and 3d: 3 + 2 = 5; 3d is filled first because of its lower n.

Resulting order:
1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s

book_ref.quote: Now, question arises that how to arrange the subshells energy wise.

blocks.prompt: 17 Calculate the (n + ℓ) values of the subshells 5d, 6s, 4f, 5p, 4d and 5s, and arrange them in the order in which they are filled. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Lower (n + ℓ) fills first; for equal (n + ℓ), lower n fills first (s: ℓ = 0, p: 1, d: 2, f: 3).

book_ref.quote: hence the order of filling subshells with electrons may be obtained from the summation

blocks.prompt: 18 State Hund's rule. Explain it with the filling of three electrons in the 2p orbitals and with the configurations of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hund's rule gives the way of filling electrons into orbitals of equal energy (degenerate orbitals), such as px, py and pz. When degenerate orbitals are available, electrons are placed in separate orbitals with the same spin rather than in the same orbital with opposite spins.

Three electrons in three p orbitals: they can be arranged (I) with two paired in one orbital and one in another, or (II) one in each of px, py and pz with the same spin. By Hund's rule (II) is correct: each orbital is singly occupied.

Reason: electrons in the same region of space repel each other because they have the same charge, so they occupy separate orbitals of a subshell to minimize repulsion; they pair only when no empty orbital is left.

Examples (Figure 2.14):
• Carbon 1s² 2s² 2p²: 2p ↑ ↑ _ → 2 unpaired electrons
• Nitrogen 1s² 2s² 2p³: 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ → 3 unpaired electrons
• Oxygen 1s² 2s² 2p⁴: 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑ → pairing starts only after each 2p orbital has one electron; 2 unpaired electrons

book_ref.quote: Which of the two is correct? The answer is given by Hund’s rule

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain how electronic configurations are represented by electrons-in-boxes diagrams, taking boron as an example. Write the configurations of chromium and copper from Table 2.7. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electrons-in-boxes diagram (Figure 2.13):
• Each box represents an atomic orbital.
• The boxes (orbitals) are arranged in order of increasing energy from bottom to top.
• An electron is represented by an arrow; the direction of the arrow represents its spin.
• When there are two electrons in an orbital their spins are opposite, so the two arrows in that box point in opposite directions.
• Electrons in the same subshell occupy separate orbitals with the same spin wherever possible, to minimize repulsion; they pair only when no empty orbital is left.

Boron (Z = 5), 1s² 2s² 2p¹: bottom box 1s ↑↓; above it 2s ↑↓; top row of three 2p boxes with one arrow ↑ in the first and two empty.

From Table 2.7 (Z = 1–36):
• Chromium (Z = 24): 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹
• Copper (Z = 29): 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s¹

book_ref.quote: A useful way of representing electronic configurations is a diagram that places electrons in boxes

blocks.prompt: 20 Explain how the electronic configurations of elements are related to their positions in the periodic table (s, p, d and f blocks). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The periodic table is structured so that elements with the same pattern of outer-shell (valence) configuration are in the same group; the configuration of an element can be written from its location (Figure 2.15). The elements are grouped by the type of orbital being filled:
• s-block: two columns on the left, the alkali metals (group 1, ns¹) and alkaline earth metals (group 2, ns²); the outer s orbitals are being filled.
• p-block: a block of six columns on the right, in which the outermost p orbitals are being filled; group 13 has ns²np¹.
• d-block: a block of ten columns in the middle containing the transition metals, in which the d orbitals are being filled.
• f-block: two rows of fourteen columns below the main table, in which the f orbitals are being filled.
The numbers 2, 6, 10 and 14 are precisely the numbers of electrons that can fill the s, p, d and f subshells.

book_ref.quote: Notice that the elements can be grouped in terms of the type of orbital into which the electrons are placed.

blocks.prompt: 21 What are valence electrons? Explain the classification of elements into representative, d-block transition and f-block inner-transition elements, and the building-up order across the periods. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell of an atom. They are primarily involved in chemical reactions, and the similarities among valence configurations account for the similar chemical properties of the elements in a group.

Classification (Figure 2.16):
• Main-group (representative) elements have valence-shell configurations nsᵃ npᵇ: the outer s or p subshell is being filled (blue area: ns; green area: np).
• d-block transition elements: a d subshell, (n − 1)d, is being filled (yellow area).
• f-block inner-transition elements: an f subshell, (n − 2)f, is being filled (light golden area).

Building-up order: period 1 fills 1s; period 2 fills 2s and then, jumping across, 2p; period 3 fills 3s and 3p; period 4 fills 4s, 3d and then 4p.

The classification of elements into metals, non-metals, representative and transition elements, periods, groups and blocks (s, p, d, f) is done on the basis of electronic configuration and valence electrons, so their chemical properties can be easily assessed.

book_ref.quote: There is a definite pattern to the order of filling of the subshells

blocks.prompt: 22 Explain how the electronic configurations of positive and negative ions are written. How do the d-block elements behave differently? Give examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Positive ions are formed when electrons are removed from atoms. E.g. Na⁺ (proton number 11) has 10 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, the same as neon.

Negative ions are formed when atoms gain electrons. E.g. S²⁻ (proton number 16) has 18 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, the same as argon.

In general, metal atoms lose electrons from the outer subshell when forming positive ions.

d-block elements: across the period from potassium to zinc the 4s subshell fills before 3d, but when a d-block atom forms an ion the 4s electrons are lost first:
• Ti atom: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d² 4s² → Ti²⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d²
• Cr atom: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ 4s¹ → Cr³⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d³

book_ref.quote: Note that, in general, electrons in the outer subshell are removed when metal atoms form the positive ions.

blocks.prompt: 23 Iron has Z = 26 (Fe: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶4s² in Table 2.7). Write the configurations of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ and find the number of unpaired electrons in Fe, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Remove 4s electrons first, then 3d; fill the five 3d orbitals singly before pairing (Hund's rule).

book_ref.quote: Reading across the Periodic Table from potassium to zinc, the 4s subshell fills before the 3d subshell.

steps: Fe²⁺ (26 − 2 = 24 electrons): both 4s electrons are lost → 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶.
Fe³⁺ (26 − 3 = 23 electrons): two 4s and one 3d electron are lost → 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵.
3d⁶: five orbitals singly filled, the sixth electron pairs in one: ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ → 4 unpaired (Fe and Fe²⁺ both have 3d⁶; 4s² in Fe is paired).
blocks.final_answer: Fe²⁺: …3d⁶; Fe³⁺: …3d⁵. Unpaired electrons: Fe 4, Fe²⁺ 4, Fe³⁺ 5.

blocks.prompt: 24 What is a free radical? Explain, with the electronic configuration of chlorine, why a free chlorine atom is a free radical, and give examples of free radicals made of groups of atoms. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Free radical: a species that has one or more unpaired electrons.

Chlorine atom Cl•: configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. The 2p subshell is full (2p⁶). In the 3p subshell there are five electrons in three orbitals: two orbitals have paired electrons whereas the third contains a single unpaired electron (3p: ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑). Because of this unpaired electron the free chlorine atom is a free radical. The unpaired electron is shown by a single dot, as in Cl•.

Groups of atoms: apart from single atoms, groups of atoms can also be free radicals, e.g. OH• and CH₃•.

book_ref.quote: An example of a simple free radical is free chlorine atom

blocks.prompt: 25 What are semiconductors? Explain, on the basis of electronic configuration, why pure silicon does not conduct, and how doping produces P-type and N-type semiconductors. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Semiconductors are materials that can conduct electricity under some conditions. They are used in many electronic devices, including smartphones, laptops and cars. Silicon, germanium and arsenic are examples of elements that can act as semiconductors; this is possible because of their unique electronic configuration.

Pure silicon: ₁₄Si = 2, 8, 4, so it has 4 electrons in its valence shell. In the pure crystalline form each Si atom is bonded to four other Si atoms (Figure 2.17), so there is no possibility of electronic conduction through the crystal.

Doping: P-type and N-type semiconductors are formed by doping the pure semiconductor with impurity atoms:
• Trivalent impurities (boron or aluminium) create a P-type semiconductor; the impurity creates holes (positive charge carriers) in the lattice.
• Pentavalent impurities (phosphorus or arsenic) create an N-type semiconductor; the impurity supplies extra electrons (negative charge carriers).

book_ref.quote: Let us consider the example of Si and explore how it can be converted into a p-type and n-type semiconductors.

blocks.prompt: 26 Describe the formation of P-type and N-type semiconductors from silicon and explain how each conducts electricity. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
P-type semiconductor: impurity atoms with three valence electrons (like Al) are added to pure silicon. Some trivalent atoms take the place of Si atoms in the crystal. The silicon atoms cannot make four bonds due to the lack of electrons, so holes are created in the crystal lattice which act as positive charge carriers (Figure 2.18). This gives a positive-type, i.e. P-type, semiconductor. Electrons from an external current source can move through it, so it acts as a conductor.

N-type semiconductor: impurity atoms with five valence electrons (like phosphorus) are added; some Si atoms are replaced by the pentavalent phosphorus atoms. The Si atoms in the vicinity can make four bonds and the fifth electron is an extra electron. These impurity atoms contribute extra electrons to the crystal lattice, which become free to move and act as negative charge carriers (Figure 2.18). The result is an N-type semiconductor that conducts electricity when connected to an external source.

book_ref.quote: For this reason, there are created holes in the crystal lattice
